extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political economy; economists; policymakers; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and explaining how the progress of wealth and agricultural improvement affects the real and nominal prices of different kinds of 'rude produce' (raw agricultural and natural products), including a threefold classification and the mechanisms driving price changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money flows to rich countries because of superior prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold and silver naturally resort to a rich country ... not because they are cheaper there than in poorer countries, but because they are dearer, or because a better price is given for them. It is the superiority of price which attracts them; and as soon as that superiority ceases, they necessarily cease to go thither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why precious metals concentrate in wealthier countries: higher offered prices (not lower relative value of metal) draw them. Use this to interpret bullion movements as driven by price differentials rather than intrinsic depreciation of the metal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal price rises reflect rises in real price, not degradation of silver
rubrics_metrics.description: Though such commodities come to exchange for a greater quantity of silver than before, it will not from thence follow that silver has become really cheaper ... It is not their nominal price only, but their real price, which rises in the progress of improvement. The rise of their nominal price is the effect, not of any degradation of the value of silver, but of the rise in their real price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observing higher money prices for goods during improvement, interpret the change as an increase in the goods' value in terms of labour/subsistence rather than as a fall in money's purchasing power. Useful when distinguishing nominal vs real price movements in historical comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold classification of rude produce (different price effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: These different sorts of rude produce may be divided into three classes: (1) those scarce to multiply by human industry, (2) those which can be multiplied in proportion to demand, (3) those in which the efficacy of industry is limited or uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to predict how prices respond to progress: each class has distinct long-run and transitional price dynamics and policy/management implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sort — naturally scarce/perishable commodities: price can rise without clear bound
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sort ... consists in those things which nature produces only in certain quantities, and which being of a very perishable nature, it is impossible to accumulate ... When wealth, and the luxury which accompanies it, increase, the demand for these is likely to increase ... their price may rise to any degree of extravagance, and seems not to be limited by any certain boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to rare birds, fishes, many game species, migratory birds, and other perishables whose supply cannot be expanded by industry. High historical prices (e.g., Roman prices for rare birds/fish) should be read as scarcity-driven rather than evidence of cheapened money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second sort — producible in proportion to demand: price rises until cultivation becomes profitable
rubrics_metrics.description: The second sort ... consists in those useful plants and animals which human industry can multiply in proportion to the demand. Their real value gradually rises, till at last it gets so high as to render them as profitable a produce as any thing else which human industry can raise upon the most fertile and best cultivated land. When it has got so high, it cannot well go higher. If it did, more land and more industry would soon be employed to increase their quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with cattle, poultry, hogs, dairy produce: prices rise with improvement until they reach a boundary where it becomes profitable to cultivate land specifically for them (e.g., turn cropland into pasture or grow feed crops). Consider constraints such as manure availability, farm stock levels, and the time required for land improvement—these slow the adjustment. Antipattern: expecting immediate supply response where capital/organic inputs and time are limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural and institutional frictions produce time-lags in adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase of stock and the improvement of land are two events which must go hand in hand, and of which the one can nowhere much outrun the other ... These natural obstructions ... cannot be removed but by a long course of frugality and industry; and half a century or a century more, perhaps, must pass away before the old system ... can be completely abolished through all the different parts of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why price-induced incentives do not immediately translate into full agricultural transformation: tenant poverty, lack of stock, need to build manure and improve land cause long transitional periods. Use when evaluating policies or historical change that rely on rapid structural adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third sort — limited or uncertain industrial efficacy: prices variable with accidents and market reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The third sort ... is that in which the efficacy of human industry, in augmenting the quantity, is either limited or uncertain. ... though the real price of this sort naturally tends to rise, yet ... it may sometimes even fall, sometimes continue the same, and sometimes rise more or less, according as different accidents render the efforts of human industry ... more or less successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes commodities that are appendages to others (e.g., wool and raw hides limited by numbers of cattle) and where external markets matter. Expect greater volatility and sensitivity to chance events; do not assume monotonic increases with improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of market (local vs international) moderates price response
rubrics_metrics.description: The market for butcher’s meat is almost everywhere confined to the country which produces it ... The market for wool and raw hides, on the contrary, is ... very seldom confined to the country which produces them. ... the market for such commodities may remain the same, or very nearly the same, after such improvements, as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing how domestic improvement affects prices, account for whether the product's market is local (prices likely to rise with domestic improvement) or international (domestic improvement may have limited effect because foreign demand/regimes dominate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete cultivation requires prices that cover rent and ordinary farming costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The lands of no country ... can ever be completely cultivated and improved, till once the price of every produce ... has got so high as to pay for the expense of complete improvement and cultivation. ... the price of each particular produce must be sufficient, first, to pay the rent of good corn land ... and, secondly, to pay the labour and expense of the farmer, as well as they are commonly paid upon good corn land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for judging whether a rise in prices is 'desirable': durable improvement and complete cultivation require prices that justify the rent, labour, and replacement of farming capital. A price that does not cover these will not sustain improvement.
